---
title: "Exercise: projections and the sinogram"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- turn a transmitted fraction $I/I_0$ into a **line integral** of the attenuation, and back,
- compute **projections** of a few point masses at a few angles, by hand,
- read a **sinogram**: sinusoids, their amplitude and phase, crossings, the 180° mirror and the constant total,
- explain why two projections do not determine an image.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked *(math)* are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

## Background

| Idea | What it means |
|---|---|
| Attenuation $\mu$ | fraction of photons removed per cm (about 0.2 cm⁻¹ for soft tissue, more for bone) |
| Measurement | $-\ln(I/I_0)$ = sum (integral) of $\mu$ along the ray |
| Line $(\theta, \rho)$ | all points with $x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho$; origin at the image centre, $y$ up, $\theta \in [0°, 180°)$ |
| Projection $p_\theta(\rho)$ | the line integrals of all parallel lines at angle $\theta$; $\theta = 0°$: column sums, $90°$: row sums |
| Sinogram | the projections side by side: $\theta$ across, $\rho$ up |
| A point $(x, y)$ | lands at $\rho = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = r\cos(\theta - \varphi)$ |

## By hand

**B1.** Beer–Lambert with numbers.
(a) A beam crosses 20 cm of water-like tissue ($\mu = 0.2$ cm⁻¹). Which fraction of the photons arrives?
(b) The beam crosses 18 cm of tissue and 2 cm of bone ($\mu = 0.5$ cm⁻¹). What is $-\ln(I/I_0)$, and $I/I_0$? Does it matter whether the bone comes first or last?
(c) A detector reads $I/I_0 = 0.05$. What is the line integral of $\mu$ along that ray?
(d) Why does a CT scanner take the logarithm of the measured intensity before doing anything else?

**B2.** Three point masses: $A = (2, 0)$ with mass 1, $B = (0, 1)$ with mass 2, $C = (-1, -1)$ with mass 1.
(a) Draw the projections at $0°$, $45°$, $90°$ and $135°$ as bar plots on a $\rho$ axis.
(b) Check that every projection sums to the same number. Which number, and why?

**B3.** The sinogram of B2.
(a) Give each point's sinusoid as $\rho = r\cos(\theta - \varphi)$: its amplitude $r$ and the angle $\varphi$ where it peaks.
(b) Sketch the three curves for $\theta$ from 0° to 180°.
(c) At which angles do two curves cross, and at which $\rho$? What does a crossing mean for the measurement?

**B4.** Where in the sinogram is (a) a point at the image centre, (b) a point at $(0, -3)$? (c) A sinogram shows a sinusoid with amplitude 5 that peaks at $\theta = 90°$. Where is the point?

**B5.** You have measured $p_{20°}(\rho)$. Without measuring again, what is $p_{200°}(\rho)$? Why does a parallel-beam scanner turn only half a turn?

**B6.** A uniform disc of radius 3 cm with $\mu = 0.2$ cm⁻¹, centred at the origin.
(a) The ray at $\rho$ crosses the disc along a chord of length $2\sqrt{9 - \rho^2}$. Compute $p_0(\rho)$ at $\rho = 0, 1, 2, 2.5, 3$ and sketch it.
(b) Does the projection depend on $\theta$? What is the area under it?
(c) The disc moves to $(2, 0)$. Sketch $p_0$ and $p_{90°}$ now. Describe its sinogram.

**B7.** A $3 \times 3$ binary image has row sums $(1, 2, 1)$ (top to bottom) and column sums $(1, 2, 1)$ (left to right).
(a) Find two different binary images with these sums.
(b) Which small change of an image never changes its row and column sums?
(c) Does a third projection at 45° always tell the images apart?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) $I/I_0 = e^{-0.2 \cdot 20} = e^{-4} = 0.018$: under 2 %.
(b) $-\ln(I/I_0) = 18 \cdot 0.2 + 2 \cdot 0.5 = 3.6 + 1.0 = 4.6$, so $I/I_0 = e^{-4.6} = 0.010$. The order does not matter: the fractions multiply, and multiplication does not care about order (after the logarithm: a sum).
(c) $-\ln 0.05 = 3.00$.
(d) Because then each reading is a **sum** of the unknowns along the ray (linear in $\mu$). Everything later (back-projection, filtering, linear systems) needs that linearity.

**B2.** (a) $\rho = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta$:

| $\theta$ | $A$ (mass 1) | $B$ (mass 2) | $C$ (mass 1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0° | 2 | 0 | −1 |
| 45° | 1.41 | 0.71 | −1.41 |
| 90° | 0 | 1 | −1 |
| 135° | −1.41 | 0.71 | 0 |

Each projection is three bars of heights 1, 2, 1 at these positions.
(b) Each sums to $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$, the total mass: a projection only moves mass sideways onto the detector, every point lands somewhere exactly once.

**B3.** (a) $A$: $r = 2$, $\varphi = 0°$ (peaks at $0°$). $B$: $r = 1$, $\varphi = 90°$. $C$: $r = \sqrt2 = 1.41$, $\varphi = -135°$, i.e. the curve $1.41\cos(\theta + 135°)$ peaks at $225°$ and has its minimum, $-1.41$, at $45°$.
(c) Set the two $\rho$ equal: $A$ and $B$ cross at $\theta = 63.4°$ ($\tan\theta = 2$), $\rho = 0.89$; $A$ and $C$ at $108.4°$, $\rho = -0.63$; $B$ and $C$ at $153.4°$, $\rho = 0.45$. At a crossing both points lie on the same ray: that projection cannot tell them apart, it shows one bar with their summed mass.

**B4.** (a) $r = 0$: the flat line $\rho = 0$. The centre of rotation is the only point that never moves on the detector. (b) $\rho = -3\sin\theta$: zero at 0°, $-3$ at 90°. (c) $r = 5$, $\varphi = 90°$: the point $(0, 5)$.

**B5.** $p_{200°}(\rho) = p_{20°}(-\rho)$: the same rays, walked in the opposite direction, so the profile is mirrored. Turning from 180° to 360° measures nothing new.

**B6.** (a) $p_0(\rho) = 0.4\sqrt{9 - \rho^2}$: 1.20, 1.13, 0.89, 0.66, 0 at $\rho = 0, 1, 2, 2.5, 3$: a half-ellipse.
(b) A disc looks the same from every direction: every projection is this half-ellipse. Area: $\mu \cdot \pi R^2 = 0.2 \cdot 9\pi = 5.65$, the total of the image.
(c) $p_0$ is the same half-ellipse centred at $\rho = 2$; $p_{90°}$ is centred at $\rho = 0$ (the disc's $y$ is 0). In the sinogram the band follows the sinusoid of the centre, $\rho = 2\cos\theta$.

**B7.** (a) For example $\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}$. Five binary images have exactly these sums.
(b) Swapping a $2 \times 2$ checkerboard: in two rows and two columns, change $\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}$ into $\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}$. Every row and column keeps its sum.
(c) No, not always: it removes some ambiguities but not all. With more angles fewer images agree with all the data. (The fourth unit counts this with the rank of a matrix.)
:::

### Math questions

**B8.** *(math)* Derive $I = I_0\exp(-\int\mu\,ds)$ from $dI/ds = -\mu(s) I$. Which assumption about the photons does the equation make?

**B9.** *(math)* From $\mathcal R f(\rho, \theta) = \int f(\rho\,\mathbf n_\theta + s\,\mathbf n^\perp_\theta)\,ds$, prove (a) the shift rule $f(\mathbf x - \mathbf t) \mapsto \mathcal R f(\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n_\theta, \theta)$, (b) the symmetry $\mathcal R f(-\rho, \theta + \pi) = \mathcal R f(\rho, \theta)$, (c) $\int \mathcal R f\,d\rho = \iint f$.

**B10.** *(math)* Show that the projection of a uniform disc (value $\mu$, radius $R$, centre 0) is $2\mu\sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}$, and check that its integral over $\rho$ is $\mu\pi R^2$.

**B11.** *(math)* A point mass $m$ at $\mathbf x_0$ is $f = m\,\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0)$. Use the first form of the definition, $\iint f\,\delta(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho)\,d\mathbf x$, to show that its Radon transform is $m\,\delta(\rho - \mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta)$, and write $\mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta$ as $r\cos(\theta - \varphi)$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B8.** Separate variables: $dI/I = -\mu(s)\,ds$, integrate from the source ($I_0$) to the detector: $\ln I - \ln I_0 = -\int\mu\,ds$. The equation says every photon has the same chance per unit length of being removed, independent of the others: one energy (otherwise $\mu$ depends on the photon) and no scattered photons reaching the detector.

**B9.** (a) $\int f(\rho\mathbf n + s\mathbf n^\perp - \mathbf t)\,ds$; write $\mathbf t = (\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n + (\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n^\perp)\mathbf n^\perp$ and substitute $s' = s - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n^\perp$: $\int f((\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n + s'\mathbf n^\perp)\,ds' = \mathcal R f(\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n, \theta)$.
(b) $\mathbf n_{\theta + \pi} = -\mathbf n_\theta$ and $\mathbf n^\perp_{\theta + \pi} = -\mathbf n^\perp_\theta$: $\mathcal R f(-\rho, \theta + \pi) = \int f(\rho\mathbf n - s\mathbf n^\perp)\,ds$, the same integral with $s \to -s$.
(c) $(\rho, s) \mapsto \rho\mathbf n + s\mathbf n^\perp$ is a rotation (Jacobian 1), so $\iint \mathcal R f\,d\rho = \iint f(\rho\mathbf n + s\mathbf n^\perp)\,ds\,d\rho = \iint f\,dx\,dy$.

**B10.** By symmetry take $\theta = 0$: the line $x = \rho$ meets the disc for $|y| \le \sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}$, so $\int f\,dy = 2\mu\sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}$. With $\rho = R\sin u$: $\int_{-R}^R 2\mu\sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}\,d\rho = 2\mu R^2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2 u\,du = \mu\pi R^2$.

**B11.** $\iint m\,\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0)\,\delta(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho)\,d\mathbf x = m\,\delta(\mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho)$ (sifting property). With $\mathbf x_0 = r(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)$: $\mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta = r(\cos\varphi\cos\theta + \sin\varphi\sin\theta) = r\cos(\theta - \varphi)$.
:::

## Explore {#explore}

The demo shows a $128 \times 128$ object on the left, with the rays of the current angle (yellow, the arrow shows the beam direction) and the detector (blue bar). The middle panel is the projection $p_\theta(\rho)$; the right panel is the sinogram, filled in up to the current angle. **Click** in the object to drop a point mass (its **mass** is set by the slider); every point gets a coloured sinusoid on the sinogram, a dashed line in the projection and a dot on the detector. **Drag moves the object** shifts the whole object instead. **0°–360°** extends the sinogram to a full turn. The readout gives the sum of the current projection, the total of the image, and each point's current $\rho$. Distances are in pixels.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="radonproj" data-preset="hand"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/radonproj.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Preset **three points by hand** (one unit of B2 = 16 pixels). Read $\rho$ of the three points at 0°, 45° and 90° (use **0°** and **+45°**) and compare with B2. What is the sum of each projection?

**E2.** Play the sinogram from 0°. At which angle do the red and green curves ($A$ and $B$) cross? What do you see in the projection at that angle? Compare with B3.

**E3.** Preset **the centre does not move**. Which curve is flat? For the other two points, read their positions in the readout and predict the amplitude and the angle of the peak of their sinusoids. Check with the slider.

**E4.** Preset **180°–360° mirrors 0°–180°**. Compare the sinogram column at 30° with the one at 210° (move the slider). What exactly is the relation? Which point has the largest amplitude, and why?

**E5.** Preset **every column has the same sum**. Read the sum of the projection at 0°, 30° and 45° and the total of the image. Are they equal? Why could they differ in the last digits on a pixel grid?

**E6.** Preset **shift the object**: drag the disc about 20 pixels to the right. How does the sinogram change? At which angles does the band move most, and at which not at all?

**E7.** Presets **Shepp–Logan sinogram** and **a real image**. In the Shepp–Logan sinogram, which feature of the phantom makes the two bright outer bands? Why are they brightest where they are tangent to the outline? Add a point mass of 8 inside the micrograph and find its curve.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** At 0°: $A$ 32, $B$ 0, $C$ −16 pixels (2, 0, −1 units). At 45°: 22.6, 11.3, −22.6 (1.41, 0.71, −1.41). At 90°: 0, 16, −16 (0, 1, −1). Every projection sums to 4.0, the total.

**E2.** They cross at about 63°: there the two point masses lie on the same ray (A at $\rho = 14.5$, B at 14.3 pixels at 63°), and the projection shows one peak holding both masses, 1 + 2 = 3, instead of two separate bars.

**E3.** The point at the centre has the flat curve $\rho = 0$. The point at $(40, 0)$ has amplitude 40 and peaks at 0°; the point at $(-20, 30)$ has amplitude $\sqrt{20^2 + 30^2} = 36.1$ and peaks at $\varphi = 123.7°$ (at 124° the readout gives $\rho = 36.0$).

**E4.** The column at 210° is the column at 30° upside down: $p_{\theta + 180°}(\rho) = p_\theta(-\rho)$, the same rays walked the other way. The point mass at $(36, 36)$ is farthest from the centre ($r = 50.9$), so its sinusoid has the largest amplitude.

**E5.** Total 1936.0; projection sums 1936.0 at 0°, 1936.8 at 30°, 1936.0 at 45°. Equal up to 0.04 %. At 0° and 90° the rays run exactly through pixel centres; at other angles the linear interpolation between pixels distributes each pixel's value over neighbouring rays not quite evenly, so the sum is exact only on average.

**E6.** Every sinusoid moves by $t_x\cos\theta + t_y\sin\theta$: with $\mathbf t = (20, 0)$ the band moves up by 20 at 0°, not at all at 90°, and down by 20 at 180°. The sinogram is bent, not slid.

**E7.** The bright outer bands come from the skull: the dense outer ring of the phantom. A ray that just grazes the ring runs a long way inside it (tangent), so its line integral is largest there. The point mass adds a thin sinusoid of its own on top of the micrograph's sinogram: linearity.
:::

## Where this leads

The sinogram is all the scanner gives us. The next unit, [back-projection](../backprojection/lec.qmd), tries the most natural inversion, smearing every projection back over the image (**back-projection**), and finds out why it blurs; the **Fourier slice theorem** explains what is missing. Later units fix the blur with a filter ([filtered back-projection](../fbp/lec.qmd)) and then treat reconstruction as a linear system ([reconstruction as a linear system](../algebraic-recon/lec.qmd)).

The same $(\rho, \theta)$ line parameters return on the Hough day: applied to a binary edge image, the Radon transform counts the edge pixels on every line, which is the Hough accumulator ([Hough lines](../hough-lines/lec.qmd)).
